A "majority" of Federal Reserve officials believed the central bank could raise interest rates if [inflation](https://www.axios.com/economy/inflation) stays high, according to [the minutes](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20260520a.htm) from the central bank's April 28-29 policy meeting. **Why it matters:**It suggests that a larger constituency than previously known is backing the possibility of _higher_ interest rates, with the fallout from the [Iran](https://www.axios.com/world/iran) war stoking quicker price increases ahead of Kevin Warsh becoming Fed chair. *   Axios [confirmed reporting](https://www.axios.com/2026/04/16/scoop-bny-openai-gpt-cyber) that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and then-Fed chair Powell last month met with Wall Street banks to discuss the risks of AI-powered attacks on bank systems. *   [About Axios](https://www.axios.com/about). *   [Advertise with us](https://www.axios.com/advertise). *   [Careers](https://www.axios.com/careers). *   [Contact us](https://www.axios.com/contact). *   [Newsletters](https://www.axios.com/newsletters). *   [Axios Live](https://www.axios.com/events). *   [Privacy policy](https://www.axios.com/legal). *   [Terms of use](https://www.axios.com/legal/terms-of-use). A majority of officials at the Federal Reserve thought higher interest rates might become necessary to combat resurgent inflation, according to minutes from the central bank’s [April meeting](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/29/business/economy/what-to-watch-at-the-federal-reserves-april-meeting.html). The record of the most recent gathering, released on Wednesday, underscored the extent to which the war with Iran has upended the economic outlook and the policy options in front of a central bank that is [on the cusp of a leadership transition](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/15/us/politics/jerome-powell-kevin-warsh-federal-reserve.html). But the energy shock stemming from the war has [pushed](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/12/business/economy/cpi-inflation-report-consumer-prices.html) inflation further away from the Fed’s 2 percent target, stoking concerns about a more persistent problem just as the labor market has [stabilized](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/08/business/economy/jobs-report-inflation-federal-reserve.html). [SKIP ADVERTISEMENT](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/20/business/economy/fed-minutes-interest-rates.html#after-story-ad-1). But three members of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee [voted against](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/01/business/economy/fed-inflation-interest-rate-dissents.html) what they described as an “easing bias” in the central bank’s policy statement. [Colby Smith](https://www.nytimes.com/by/colby-smith) covers the Federal Reserve and the U.S. economy for The Times.
